newsitem.title: USA: Anthony Lake's exit marks new CIA setback.
newsitem.headline: Anthony Lake's exit marks new CIA setback.

text.p: The withdrawal of President Bill Clinton's choice as chief spymaster dealt a new blow to the Central Intelligence Agency, already reeling from a long series of embarrassments.

Anthony Lake's decision to ask Clinton on Monday to pull his name from consideration for the job highlighted the many nagging headaches that plague the spy agency as it marked its 50th birthday this year -- leaderless and its post-Cold War mission no longer clear.

Morale has been in tatters by most insider accounts, undermined by the discovery of two confessed spies for Moscow in CIA ranks, frequent changes at the top, botched operations in allied countries and scandals in Central America.

In the past two years, covert operations have run afoul of generally friendly local authorities in Germany, France, Italy and India. Operations against President Saddam Hussein of Iraq, a key target, collapsed in September 1996 after Saddam attacked a Western-protected Kurdish enclave.

The spy agency, the crown jewel of the $30 billion a year U.S. intelligence empire, has also been under siege for its dealings with shady characters in Guatemala, Honduras and alleged tolerance of drug-running by Latin American allies.

In a fresh blow that may have sealed Lake's decision to to withdraw, the CIA said on Monday that it had opened an internal investigation into "extremely serious" charges of improper contacts between agency personnel and Clinton's Democratic party on behalf of a controversial political donor.

The CIA investigation sought to untangle how the donor, Roger Tamraz, managed to attend several meetings with Clinton despite red flags raised by aides to Lake, Clinton's national security adviser from 1993 to 1997.

Lake, in a letter to Clinton on Monday, said he lost patience after learning that the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee planned to delay his confirmation vote over access to his FBI files and questions about aides' contacts with campaign donors.
"If this were a game, I would persist until we won," Lake wrote Clinton. But he said the future of the CIA was at stake.

"The Agency, once again, is becoming politicized. The longer this goes on, the worse the damage. The controversy and its effects could linger on after my confirmation. The men and the women of the CIA deserve better than this," Lake said.

The day before Lake withdrew, Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, the New York Democrat who served as vice chairman of the intelligence committee from 1981 to 1985, said the CIA already was in a state of "institutional collapse" because of the search for its fifth director in six years.

Among those mentioned as possible replacements were acting CIA Director George Tenet, a one-time Lake aide on the National Security Council staff and former staff director of the intelligence committee, and Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick, considered for the post before Lake was tapped.
Another possible candidate was Frank Wisner, the U.S. ambassador to India and son of one of the CIA's founders and most celebrated intelligence officers.
Lake, 57, was nominated to succeed John Deutch, who left in December after 20 months, saying a longer term was necessary to enact badly needed CIA reforms.

Clinton's first CIA director, James Woolsey, resigned with the White House's blessing in December 1994 after becoming ensnared in the case of CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames and finding he was largely shut out of access to the president.

Before persuading Deutch to take Woolsey's job, Clinton nominated yet another man in 1995 -- retired Air Force General Michael Carns. He suddenly bowed out amid questions about the accuracy of visa information he provided to bring a Filipino housekeeper to Washington.
Woolsey compared the job of director of central intelligence to being "a skunk at a garden party."
"You're always telling people things that they don't want to hear -- sometimes that their policies aren't working," he said.
